comments.body:
> **Marcus** · cohort peer

Blunt version: do not lead with the corpus. Lead with the measurement.

Nobody asks "is the data fake" about a project whose headline is *"I built an evaluation harness that blocks a merge on a metric regression."* They ask it about a project whose headline is *"I built a RAG system."* The first is a claim about your engineering; the second invites a question about your data.

replies.body:

comments.body:
Marking this as the answer since it is the framing question rather than a technical one, and getting it wrong costs people interviews.

**The reframe: synthetic is a methodological choice, and you should say so first.**

The defensive answer is *"it is synthetic, but…"*. The correct answer is that you chose it, on purpose, for a reason that is hard to argue with:

> "The corpus is generated from a fact graph, which means the gold labels are **true by construction** — there is no annotation-error floor underneath any number I report. On a hand-labelled set, a 2-point recall difference can be annotator disagreement. On this one it cannot be. That was the point: I wanted to teach measurement, and measurement is unteachable if the ground truth is itself uncertain."

That is not a defence. It is a reason a careful person would make the same choice.

**Then volunteer the limitation before they ask**, which is what actually builds credibility:

> "What it does *not* give me is distributional realism. Real corpora have duplicates, contradictions, OCR noise and documents that are wrong. My retriever never had to survive any of that, and I would expect the absolute numbers to move on a real corpus. What transfers is the harness — the metrics, the eval-set construction, the CI gate — not the constants."

**Why this works.** You have demonstrated the thing panels are actually screening for: **knowing which parts of your own result generalise.** A candidate who defends their numbers as universally valid is a risk. A candidate who says "the method transfers, the constants do not" is describing how they will behave on the client's data, which is the only thing the interview is really about.

**Two failure modes to avoid.**

- **Over-apologising.** "It's only synthetic, so it's not really representative" concedes more than is true and invites them to discount the whole project.
- **Over-claiming.** Do not say it is "like production data". It is not, they know it is not, and one sentence of over-claim costs you the credibility of everything else you said.

**If you have thirty extra minutes before the interview**, the strongest possible version of this is to run the harness against a real corpus — [MultiHop-RAG](https://github.com/yixuantt/MultiHop-RAG) plugs into the same record schema, and notebook 02 documents the mapping. Then the answer becomes *"I ran it on both; here is what moved and what did not"*, and the question stops being a challenge and becomes the most interesting thing you said.
